And then Pavle, he was the most important person. He was walking round the villages on a daily basis looking for weapons, saying it had to be surrendered. People who had hunting rifles. There were no other weapons except hunting rifles. And he said whoever didn't give in their weapons would be executed. And everyone went to give up their weapons so as to avoid being executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there a particular day when he came to your village which you saw him in possession of a list containing the names of Muslims that he was looking for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Maybe the second or third day of that operation, I went there and sat with them. My brothers were there. There were barracks there. They were taking showers there. And about ten days later, my wife was in Sarajevo, my youngest son was in the house. He was cooking beans. I told him, "Make some beans," because my wife was not there. And we went to dig the fields. And then on my meadow, young boys play ball. And I didn't pay any attention. And when the shooting started from a hill close to the Drina, I saw well --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were they shooting at you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: -- that bullets were falling close to my legs. I don't know, but the bullets were falling round my legs. And let me just add, there was a pear tree, and I was digging close to the pear tree. I approached the pear tree, and I found a bullet in the pear tree. I knew my son was in the house and he would get killed by this large column of soldiers. I threw down my hoe and ran to the house to save my child, and my neighbours said, "The one who is sitting there with us every day," they said, "Hold on to this old man." And a small young soldier was holding a pipe, and he said, "Let's set his house on fire." But I said I had served the army in Belgrade and everywhere and that he was familiar with Serbia. And this soldier said, "Don't do that." When they sat down - Pavle was their commander, this Pavle - he asked me, "Do you, old man, have any rakija?" Then another one said, "Are there any Serb villages around?" And I said, "Yes, close by." And then they asked, "Did any Muslims get killed or did any house get burnt?" And I said, "No." And then they said, "The SDA party keeps saying that the Muslims are getting killed." And I said, "That is not true. We're sitting together every day." Then we brought some walnuts and gave them these walnuts to eat. And he was holding this list, and he was mentioning people who were in various parties and who used to be in the police. And when we were leaving the stadium, Ojdanic read out himself and said, "Is such-and-such a person here?" And all these people came up to Ojdanic. And I said, "Why should I be held responsible for those people when you had released them down there at the stadium?" Then there was a cave somewhere down there which I had never seen. And then my son went to my brother's, and then there was a pair of shoes and he tore them opening looking for something inside. And then there was one of them from Serbia wearing a fur hat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. 116. I just want to clear up some things you're speaking about. You began to say that somebody in the group among the soldiers said, "Let's burn his house down." Were they referring to your house, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I calmed them down. I said that I had been a soldier in Belgrade. I know all the towns and villages. So they sat down, and they ate those walnuts, and then they took out this list and mentioned the cave, and they asked me if I had any weapons. I said I didn't have any. Then he talked to me at length. He said, "Give up your weapons. They'll kill you." I said, "I don't have any." And then he asked where this other brother of mine was or, rather, my son, and Paja [phoen] said, "What son? What son?" I said, "He's my son. He's gone to cook lunch. I don't know where he is." "He's a hostage. If you don't bring that son, this one is done for." And he said, "Where will I find you?" And he said, "You know where our headquarters are." And then they took my son.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. 116, at one point did these men take your older son into custody? Yes or no, if you can answer it that way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Those same people, yes, they took this son in front of the house. Then I followed them to see them off. This was my custom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask you another question. Did they make it -- or did they try to make a deal with you regarding your oldest son? Did they try and make an arrangement to ask you to bring your youngest son to them as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Yes. They ordered that if I don't bring this son, they would kill this other one, the one they were taking down there, and that they would come the next day to set fire to the whole village and kill everyone. So I saw them off part of the way, and then a soldier, they called him Zaric, said, "It's better to get one killed than two." So I went back and I called this son of mine who had run away to the wood. And this neighbour of mine, Fadil, was with him. They were playing ball. He said, "Father, why are you calling me?" And I said that I had to take him down there. And he said, "You want to take me to get killed." And I said I had to. And Fadil said, "Better take him down there. It's better to do that than have the whole village burned down, because they'll blame us, and this way there will be fewer victims." So I went after them to the place where they told me the headquarters were. I found two officers playing cards, and Pavle was there. And I said, "Comrade Commander, I've brought two young men."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. 116. Did you bring your other son to a place where Muslims were brought to be interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: I brought them to the place where Pavle had told me to bring them, this other son, because if I hadn't, he said that they would burn down the whole village. And he said to a soldier, "Take him over there." And there was a holiday home nearby. They would interrogate them there and then send them to the prison in Visegrad. And I appealed to the man who was called Zaric, and I said, "Zaric, they'll kill my son. Please go and protect him." And he cursed everybody and said that was all wrong. He ran down the road to the stable, and Zaric went to this weekend home, and then a military van appeared from town, and I saw the van, how they picked them up and they took them off to Visegrad, to the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. 116, did there come a time when you were able to convince them to release your sons? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: At the time up there near the house do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At the time you went to the place of interrogation. Were you able to get your son released from that place of interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: I went to my sister's when they took this younger one, but the older one wasn't there. He wasn't where they said he would be. Pavle tricked me. Then I took a directory, and I called up as many people as I knew to get my son out of prison. And I can't say now, but one man said to me that they would be released. He said I wasn't -- "I'm not commander of the prison, but I will certainly release them, even at the cost of my own life." I spent two days at my sister's, and again I called his wife and his son, and then my sister said, "Go home. Your wife is not there. You have the livestock to tend to, and the man said he would release them." Then my wife came back and she was crying, and then first Fadil came and then later this young man came, and then later my son, the second -- both the first and the second one were released. They released 14 of them, not just my children, that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. 116, you mentioned that -- that these men threatened to burn down the entire village if you did not bring your sons to this place. Was your village burnt down that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Well, I took him there. That's what he said. He said, if I didn't take the younger son -- that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was your village burnt down that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: No, because I took him off. I carried out his order.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when your house was burnt down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: We were in the woods for many months hiding. Each house had five or six bunkers from the shells on the right-hand side of the Drina. We had some binoculars. The right side is close by, and every second or third day, military trucks from Uzice would come in bringing mortars and shells, and the artillery was set up from the Visegradska Banja downwards, tanks, tops. And we saw them bringing in the tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. 116, was there a time that your house was burnt down? If you can answer that yes or no, I'd appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Not straight away. When we withdrew from all the villages, that's when, but we hid there for a very long time in the woods from the five villages or ten villages, all us people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. 116, is it correct that all of the houses in your village were burnt down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: There's not a single one standing. You don't know where they were, where they used to be. You can't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did all those houses in your village belong to Muslim families?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Yes, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. 116.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, let me ask you first of all something about the last thing you said, what you've just said. How much time was it all after the events with the officer and when your son was taken off and when your house and the other houses were set fire to? How much time had gone by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Well, a lot of time had gone by, because we were all in the woods. We had taken to the woods. Some of the houses were shelled and destroyed, and no houses were left standing, not even sheds. There was nothing standing. Everything was razed to the ground. On Saturday, for the people who came up for the weekends, they hit us all the time. The recruits from Uzice came, and the artillery came, sir, but they handed in their weapons on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you to answer my questions, please, what I'm asking you, and try and be specific and give specific answers. Let us repeat. You said that your house and the village was set fire to later on, while you were in hiding. How long afterwards was that, after your son had been taken and released? How many days or months, if it was a long period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: We were in the woods and a lot of time went by. We had our bunkers in the woods. We saw that we couldn't stay there. And then later on, there were some people who stayed on, but I can't remember who they were. They stayed in the woods, some of them. But there was a strong offensive from the army at our villages, and that's when all the houses were burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood your answer. I wasn't able to follow you exactly. Well, let me ask you something else. Do you remember the day when the Uzice Corps left the Visegrad area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know that I would come here for me to remember all those dates and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I didn't mean the date, I meant do you remember the departure of the Uzice Corps, when the Uzice Corps left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: I remember that they left. They were there for a time. How long they were there, I really can't say. I don't remember. And when they left, when they went back, I was interested in who had left the guns there to fire at us and the trucks with the ammunitions. That's what I'm interested in, who sent the young soldiers to be trained there and sent all the ammunition and everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, look, sir, please, you really must just answer the question. If there is something that the Prosecution wants you to add to your answer later, they will be able to ask you, but at the moment, just answer the question which Mr. Domazet asked you. He said, "Did you remember the departure of the Uzice Corps?" And you have said, "Yes." Now, that's the answer to it. Now, you ask your next question, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The burning the houses, your own and the other houses in the village, did that take place the day after the Uzice Corps left Visegrad? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Afterwards. Afterwards. When the army column went to ransack the villages, that's when it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let us go back to the first day, the day that you were transferred to Visegrad in the truck. Let's look at that day. According to what you told us today, it wasn't quite clear to you why you were being taken to Visegrad; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I didn't know why I was being taken to Visegrad. I apologise for being a little nervous a moment ago. All we knew was that they were taking us off to be killed. When we look at the photographs from Bijeljina, and the pictures from Bijeljina, everybody thought that that would happen to us, that we would never return, and that's why I went to set the livestock free, to let the cattle out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In your village, (redacted) I think it's called --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: With the army, did VG22 come? You know who VG22 is? He's a witness. Did he come too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Yes. He was there. That witness was there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What did he say at the time? Did he tell you to go to Visegrad with the army? Did he call you to go with the army to Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Yes, he did. I was -- we were trying to save ourselves, and that's when I left and went to let my cattle out, because I didn't know if I would return. The people kept asking him, pleading with him. They said, "If we leave the Drina, it won't be a good thing. If we stay in the woods" -- our villages were up there, all the weapons and clothing as somebody had given them weapons and clothing to these Orthodox people. That's why we escaped this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Witness 22, therefore, was in the village with the army, and he called upon you and the other inhabitants to go to Visegrad with the army; is that right? Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: I don't see seem to remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that he talked to you and that he spoke about the fact that you should go to Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: He said that we should go to Visegrad. The people told him to look out for our safety because we didn't know what to do or where to go. So the people asked this person, 22, to look out for our safety and to see what we should do, and he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You knew Witness 22, didn't you, personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I knew him personally. He was with us in the column going off towards the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is he a relative of yours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What kinship relations do you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: He is my brother's son.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you are his uncle.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At that time --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: He was with the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Please let me finish my question before you answer, Witness. Do you know that he was a prominent functionary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Yes, he was. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And Witness 22 also went with you and the people in the trucks towards Visegrad; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned a moment ago, and I think that this led to some misunderstanding, that you were brought to the station, the bus station or what used to be the railway station; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Yes. I went to let out the cattle and then down to the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm asking you about Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Well, I went across the bridge, and the whole column did, and then you reach the station right after the bridge up there. I can show you on the -- I can't show you on the map because I can't see those small lines, those thin lines. I can't see the details on the map for me to be able to point them out to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is it true that the station is located right by the city stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, just a little to the left. The stadium for all the matches is just a little to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you arrived at the station in the trucks, there were a lot of people in the stadium, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Yes. More than half the stadium was already full. I didn't ask how they had reached the stadium across the Drina River from the right-bank villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So that meeting wasn't at the station in fact, it was at the stadium next to the station; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Yes, it was at the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And you then saw an officer arriving by helicopter, that he talked to you later on, addressed you, and that he was addressed as Ojdanic, that his name was Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And the soldiers surrounded him when he arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did he say that you could return to your villages, that is to say, the villages that you mentioned that they said were safe or liberated, which was the term you used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Well, we didn't know what was going to happen to us, so we asked them what to do, whether we could go to the nearby villages. And they said, "Well, wait a little while." And number 22, Witness 22, was next to him, and he said, "We just have to take care of something." And they lined up the soldiers, and the soldiers searched our belongings. When this was completed, when the search was completed, he said, "(redacted), Musici, Jelacici, all the nearby villages have been liberated. You can go home now." That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You've already told us that. Now, you spoke about the search your belongings. Did they look for weapons or did they confiscate other things as well? Did he they loot the people or did they just check for weapons and then let you be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: No, they didn't loot us. They didn't loot our belongings. The soldiers didn't loot us. I didn't see them looting. I personally didn't see them looting. That's what I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, what were they looking for then? What were they looking for when they searched you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, because they searched the women, too, in the way that wasn't really very nice. It wasn't as it should have been. It wasn't in order. People just had small bags and some food. People didn't have any weapons, and they had collected up all the hunting rifles that people had had and handed in. What they were looking for, I have no idea, actually. But they did do a lot of searching. They searched through our shoes as well. They looked inside. Why, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but you didn't notice them confiscating anything, taking anything from the people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: I did not notice anything, no. I personally didn't. I stood along the fence of the stadium. I wanted to make myself scarce. I was afraid. So I tried to get as far away as possible. Perhaps somebody else saw what they were doing and what their behaviour was like. I personally didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At that particular time prior to the meeting at the stadium, did most of the population flee from Visegrad? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: You mean before they arrived?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, that's right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Lots of people left Visegrad many people. They went where they could. Everybody looked out for themselves from the military department and lots and lots of people fled because they saw that they would come to Visegrad. And my two villages, Gornja and Donja --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Sir, please answer my questions as I ask them, as I put them to you. Did you hear about the hydroelectric power plant problem, that somebody was in control of the dam and that they wanted to release the water from the dam, and was that the reason why most of the -- why all of these people wanted to leave Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Well, I can't know that. I know that there was a man called Murat at the hydroelectric power plant and that the soldiers went up there to guard the place that the corps went up there to the power plant. There might have been some other people as well at the power plant, maybe some other people as well. Everybody had heard that he wanted to release the water.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand you. Did you hear that he wanted to release the water from the dam and that that was the problem?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Nobody would flee from the water, no, not from the water. We were afraid. Everybody was afraid because we knew, more or less, that they would occupy Visegrad, and a lot of weapons had been given up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't ask you about any weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG116
utterances.text: Well, the people didn't flee from the water from the dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That is the end of your task here. Thank you for coming to give the evidence. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you all, too, and I am very happy to have seen you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, when you and your co-counsel want to discuss things, perhaps you could remove the earphones and then you don't have to shout.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. I told him just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, before you go, I know people have different styles of taking witnesses, but if I may suggest to you the best for the witness like is to say to him - and you must have discovered this is what he was going to be like when you spoke to him earlier - is to say to him, "Just answer my question and I'll take you through the story." If you just let them talk, we are inundated with irrelevancy. But if you take him and say, "What happened on this day? Where did you go? Who did you speak to?" you'll get through it very much more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said that many times to him -- I said that to him many, many times yesterday. I think just the excitement of being present here in the Tribunal, he was off on running.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It is, if I may say so, a general style of examination that you pursue and it is very much more efficient if you do interrupt them and ask questions. You may not have been able to control that witness. By the way, we were talking at some stage about your five best witnesses; I assume you have exhausted them, have you, on the issue of attacks on the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You were going to limit your -- the number of witnesses you were going to call on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Much of the evidence that was brought out through Mr. Domazet's questions I purposely did not go into those topics with the witness. The only points I wanted to bring out with this witness were the paper and the -- so we have made an effort. We have struck some of the witnesses off and any of the witnesses that are talking about matters that have already been introduced into evidence, we are not asking them questions on in our case in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He had new material on persecution, I realise that, but I hope we've now finished calling witnesses solely upon the issue of an attack upon the Muslim population, because there hasn't been any real dispute about it, so far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, whose your next witness? Mr. Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the next witness is Mr. Mevsud Poljo, Mevsud Poljo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, will you make the solemn declaration in the document which the usher is showing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Mr. Mevsud Poljo, could you confirm your name. Could you tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Mevsud Poljo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Where and when were you born?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: On the 4th of May, in the village of Vlahovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Where is that village located?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: That village is 15 kilometres away from Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: At the moment, I have a private business, private enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1995 -- 1991 and the beginning of 1992, where were you living?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: I lived in the village of Vlahovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: At that time, had barricades been set up on the main road between Prelovo and Zupa?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Yes, they had. There were several barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Do you have any idea as to why the barricades were set up?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Tensions were growing between the Serbian and Bosniak or Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: After the barricades had been set up, did you leave your village?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: The barricades were set up a month before. I didn't leave the village. I passed the barricades. They were mostly manned during the night. During the day, they were dismantled.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: In 1992, did you, nevertheless, leave your village at some point?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In 1992, I was among the first to leave my village, and it was sometime in March, I think. I'm not quite sure. Maybe April. I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: It was a mixed population, and some shooting started. There were disturbances. Our villages were attacked during the night. Different weapons were used, small calibre rifles. There was shooting from small-calibre rifles. Our houses were shot at, and the borderline villages, and the people were afraid and fled to the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Which destination did you take when you fled from your village? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: I went towards Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: And at Zepa, which locality were you living in?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: I lived in a small village called Slap, on the banks of the Drina River. That is to say, I had crossed over into that village, the village of Slap, and I stayed there until the autumn of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Can you tell us the distance, approximate distance between Zepa and Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: It's about 20 kilometres. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: At Slap, in the Zepa region, did you have an occupation of any kind?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Which?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: As the dam was released and the Drina had flooded the area and when the Drina retreated to its riverbed, there was a lot of mud and sludge and slush that was left over. So I and a neighbour of mine went off with two vehicles to Slap, and we weren't able to cross, to approach the Drina, because the boats were on the other bank. And we called to them to come to our bank, and we cleaned on our side, they cleaned on their side. And they told us what the situation was like in Zupa, in the place that I was from. Can I continue? May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: When we had cleaned this area up and were able to approach the Drina, the river, then we took up some boats and we told the people from Zepa that all the people from Zupa would have to leave and that they ought to empty some of their houses so that they could take in the people that were coming in. The people weren't able to remain where they were because they were threatened. There was this great threat. So they asked them to evacuate a few houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: While you were carrying out this task, were you part of a group that was pulling out bodies from the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Yes. For several days, we would carry our relatives and neighbours across the river. We would transport them across the river. And when we crossed to the other side, I was given the task of being night watchman on the Drina bank, at the lake itself, together with other locals from Zepa. I carried out that task. For about a month I was on watch duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Where were these bodies coming from that you pulled out of the river?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: The bodies were coming from Visegrad, downstream.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: When did you see those bodies floating for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: One body, the first one, arrived in mid-May. It was an elderly man who had no documents on him. All he had was some prescriptions and medicines for diabetes, as he suffered obviously from diabetes. And then we had connections with Rogatica. Rogatica was the municipality for Zepa. And then the police and judges came from Rogatica. They pulled out the body and processed it according to a procedure, the name of which I don't know. And then other bodies started arriving in June and July.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: For how long did you continue to perform this function, so to speak, this role?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: I think I stayed until October of that same year. September or October.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: How many bodies were you able to pull out together with your comrades during that period?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: As far as I now remember, we pulled out 170 or 180 bodies, and after I left, I think there were more. Another 10 or 15, as far as I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: What were they, these bodies? What was your role in this group?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: I was a member of a group. There were two or three gentlemen whose task was to row the boat without an engine and also to pull out the bodies during night-time and early in the morning before it became light. So I think the person who collected most of the bodies was a young imam, a hodza, Muratagic. I now forget his first name. He alone pulled out more than half of those bodies. I think up to a hundred. As for my role, my role was once the bodies were taken out of the water, to try and identify them, to search them. There were five other men who were searching them, taking out objects from their pockets and everything else they found on them. And we worked in such a way that if we found a document, an ID document or a passport or a health card or a driving licence, we wouldn't go on searching the body but we would immediately bury it in a pit not very deep, about 30 centimetres deep. Depending on whether there were several bodies, we had to dig deeper and so on. It depended on the number of bodies we had to bury. And I would write the description, if we knew who it was, the date of birth and other particulars. If we didn't know, if there were no documents on the body, then we would describe it, saying how the person was killed, and we would describe any clothing or shoes or anything that we found on him, and then we would put in a bag those objects and keep them safely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Could you tell us the percentage of men, women, and children among the bodies that you pulled out of the river?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Women, as far as I can now remember -- sometimes I was absent. I would go to fetch food, because I would also hunt game. So I think there may have been not more than ten. Seven or eight women, as far as I can remember, and the rest were men, about 160 or 170 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did you say the rest were men or women?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: When I asked you the question as to the percentage share of women, men, or children among the bodies, if you can remember that ratio. Maybe it was due to the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I guess it must have been, Mr. Ossogo. The English translation is very clear. The witness said, "Seven or eight women, as far as I can remember, and the rest were men, about 160 or 170 of them."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: And what general condition were they in? I'm not asking you for the specific condition of each individual, but the general condition in which you found those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: May I just explain this? I said that there were 160 or 170 men and that there were women, seven or eight, not more than ten. Did I make myself clear? As for children - you asked me about children - two or three small children of a few months old.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: It's quite clear now, Mr. Poljo. But to go back to the last question that I asked you. What was the general condition of the bodies that you pulled out of the Drina?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: The bodies we pulled out of the Drina were in a very bad condition. They had been mutilated. It's hard to describe. I can start from the head. There were 15 or 16 bodies with half their heads missing, several bodies without one eye, some didn't have both eyes. There were broken arms and legs. There were bodies that were black and blue, beaten up on the back and the chest. There were a couple of bodies with their genitals cut off. I remember one or two bodies that had their sexual organ cut off. Then their testes were hanging loose, up to their knees. In any event, they had been beaten up. Those that we examined and that we stripped naked, those were the ones that didn't have any documents on them. As for those that had documents, we didn't look further. We immediately buried them because there was shelling, we were in a hurry, it was hot, the bodies were stinking. For three months you couldn't approach the Drina River because of the stench.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Were you able to pull out all the bodies or were there bodies that you were unable to pull out for any reason, for one reason or another? At first we really didn't know what to do for a couple of days. Those bodies went by. They flowed down the river. And then we sort of tried to organise ourselves. I was the one who took the initiative, that we should try to pull out some bodies. I had two brothers and an uncle and some relatives employed. So while I was on guard duty, I saw these bodies passing by, and then we agreed that we should try and pull out as much as we could, but we pulled out perhaps 20 per cent of the bodies. The rest flowed by. We were able to pull them out only during night-time and early in the morning while there was still a mist, because the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Were there bodies that were so decomposed that you were unable to deal with them?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: There were bodies that stank so much, as if they had been in a washing machine. They were all broken up. I remember two small children, two or three months old. They were in a plastic bag and then in a jute bag. And when we pulled out those bags, we tore them open with a Gillette, and we saw they were babies, and we didn't want to do anything. There was a naked baby. I was in the boat when we tried to pull it out, and we just couldn't. So we let it flow down the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: So the bodies that you were able to pull out and examine were in a relatively acceptable state, to put it that way?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Could you describe to us the condition in which -- the condition of the first body that you were able to take out?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: The first body, the one that arrived sometime in May, I was present all the time while the description was being done. I couldn't notice anything, whether he had been killed or whether he had thrown himself into the river. I don't remember any evidence of any blows or any fractures on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did this body have his genitals out or any organs broken?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: I was speaking about the man whose -- that is, the body that reached us in May, And it was in June and July that bodies came on a daily basis. First some bodies flowed by, and then we managed to catch some that had their skulls broken up to their eyes. There was no brain left, and small fish were entering the cavities in their heads. And their legs had been broken. Some had one leg. I don't know which.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: This body that was in such a condition was pulled out in the month of June, wasn't it, more or less, roughly?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: In June, the bodies were in a worse condition. But later on, as time went by, in the summer, the bodies came in a very bad condition. So I think that most of the crimes that occurred occurred in June. Seventy or 90 per cent in June and then in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Could you describe the condition of the body of a woman whose tongue had been torn out?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Yes. I remember there was a youngish woman, under 30, that was naked and wrapped up in a blanket, and her tongue had been pulled out and tied with some wire or something and tied to the side, towards her ear, with cord or a wire. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Were you able to pull out of the Drina bodies of women wrapped up in sheets, but several bodies at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion, I think there were two younger women and a woman of some 50. So two under 30 and one of 50 who came in that condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Were you able to identify to whom those sheets belonged? Was it to an individual or an institution?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: As regards this one young woman, she came later, wasn't it? Three or four women came at once. One was a young girl, I think she was, a young woman, and her name was, or surname, rather, I think it was Smajic or Smajlovic. She came from a village close to mine. Lasci or something like that, village of Lasci. And this young woman arrived together -- she was clothed, nicely dressed. We found on her, in her leather jacket, a passport belonging to another young woman who was working abroad. I think it was in Austria. And we buried her. We just took the documents. And she had some money on her, wrapped around her waist. She had sewn some money into her clothing. When we had finished all that, we had said who it was, and the story was, as parents would come there daily, women looking for their husbands, checking to see whether they could recognise anyone, and when we said about this young woman, they said it was not true, that that young woman was alive, that she had crossed somewhere up there the village of Luka, I think, that she had crossed into Luka and that she was alive there, that this could have been someone else. Then the brother or father, anyway, relatives of that young woman came together with that girl who was alive, and it had to do with the documents. She was afraid because she had worked abroad, and she had given her her documents and this money so as not to be killed, and this other woman was very poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Poljo. I would like to know, for the record, the colour of those sheets. You spoke of three women that you pulled out of the river, and they were wrapped up in sheets.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Yes. Two other youngish women and an older woman. One was younger and the other older. As if they were mother and daughter, they were in blankets. They were wrapped in blankets. And there was another older woman, but I think that was later. I think it was my aunt. She arrived that same day. The blankets, they were multicolored. I think they were brown in colour. Mostly they were brown in colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Could those blankets have belonged to a hotel?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: As we found the documents on this girl and as they arrived on the same day, a couple of hours later, I had been to the Vilina Vlas Hotel, and I knew, when I was visiting a relative there - and there are other people who confirmed this - that these blankets could have come from the Vilina Vlas Hotel. This young woman had to pass by that hotel. These other two women on whom we found no documents, these people recognised them as neighbours. I think they used to work for Smajlovic. She came from Kamenica, and she was the sister or daughter of a forester, and she had married into this Lasci village, and she had to pass by that hotel. So this was another element that was taken into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did you pull out bodies from the Drina on which there were traces of bullets or firearms?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: Yes. I remember two men. They were not neighbours, but I knew them well. One of them had worked on my house. I can't recollect just now. His name was Hamed Kresmer and Ibrahim Kresmer. They were killed in the easiest way. They just had one bullet hole in the chest. One had one in the chest and the other one had one in the neck. They were well dressed, clean, the bodies were fresh. They had cigarettes on them, All the documents, as if they were on their way to a party. They were clean-shaven, only they had gone stiff and their arms were raised upwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Were you able to see any traces of abuse on the legs or bodies of females?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: We described everything the way we found it. There were traces on the chest and the neck of one young woman, and this other one as well, the one came previously. I don't remember whether they had been killed with a weapon or something like that or that they had any fractures. They could only have been strangled or poisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You said a little earlier that there were objects that you took from the bodies and recorded. What was the general condition of those objects? The clothing, were they in civilian clothing or possibly in military clothing?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO
utterances.text: The objects, I consider objects to be lighters, for instance. I think that there were empty wallets. There were a lot of those. Then there were some medical booklets, a passport here and there, a driving licence. There were prescriptions, documents, titles to land. There was some photographs. A couple of bodies were found with some money on them. I remember that a man had 500 German marks on him. He was from a place called Varnice. And the girl that I mentioned a moment ago, she had some money on her too. So there were some small objects. I remember a man who had five or six watches, pocket-watches on a chain. And then a body or two would have a wristwatch on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Ossogo, it's 4.00. We'll adjourn now until 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
